title: Rob Schneider leans on faith, holds hope for reconciliation with estranged daughter Elle King
summary: Rob Schneider discusses Christianity, forgiveness, and a higher power as he navigates his strained relationship with daughter Elle King on a podcast.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Rob Schneider's relationship with estranged daughter Elle King may be strained, but he has hope for the future.
Schneider, 62, admitted on Andrew Gold's "Heretics" podcast that he'll always be there for the "very talented" country singer despite challenges with the past.
The "Grown Ups" actor recalled a previous public appearance where he admitted he "wasn't the dad" that his daughter needed.
KELSEY GRAMMER URGES AMERICANS TO LOOK TO FOUNDING FATHERS FOR GUIDANCE AS NATION FACES DEEP DIVISIONS
Elle King doesn't regret sharing her childhood experiences as the daughter of comedian Rob Schneider. (Getty Images)

"I wasn't prepared emotionally for the outpouring of what I received after that," Schneider said. "There's an endemic – and I don't know if in other cultures, but in the United States – an endemic of kids who went off to college and came back and said, 'My daughter doesn't want to have a relationship with me anymore,' or, 'I can't see my grandkids.'"
"It's an attack on the culture in a way that the culture is vulnerable."

In 2024, King shared insight into her at-times "toxic" childhood during an appearance on BunnieXO's "Dumb Blonde" podcast. King confessed that her dad was "just not nice" and would go "four or five years without talking" to her.
"I put out my record and people finally started asking about my dad," she said. "My dad called me, and was like, ‘Don’t f---ing talk about me in the press.'"
DENISE RICHARDS SAYS SAMI 'STANDS UP' TO DAD CHARLIE SHEEN AND THAT HE NEEDS IT

She remembered, "If I would ever spend a summer with my dad, it would be on a movie set. I would just get lost in the shuffle. If I ever messed up a shot, if I ever was talking, like, I would get in f---ing trouble."
Elle King shared details about growing up as the daughter of actor Rob Schneider on Bunnie XO's podcast. (Getty Images)

"He also didn't have a very good reputation. I don't want to be associated with him. He's just not nice. You can want someone to change so much; you can't control anyone else's actions. You can't control people's feelings. All you can control is how you react and what you do with your feelings, and sometimes I f---ing boil up, and I boil over and I f---ing bust my lid."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

King added, "You try every different angle. I would try letters. I would try soft. I would try yelling … my dad forgot about every single birthday. I spent my 18th birthday in a summer school, and they brought me cupcakes, and I came home and my dad forgot my birthday."
Schneider later apologized for the past, and admitted he wasn't sure if his daughter accepted his words.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"The door's open, and I would say, you know, I love you and ... I'm there when you want," he said. "We had an exchange, and I'll leave it at that. The thing about, as a parent, you just have to love and be available and be an open door. My door's always open."

He added, "The second she needs me, I'll be there. That's all you can do, and the idea that I'm going to somehow ... that I need something, that I can force my way or force ... no. It has to be something that ... an openness."
Schneider conveyed the importance of recognizing a "higher power" to help guide him through difficult times.
Rob Schneider reflected on his relationship with his daughter on the "Heretics" podcast. (Jason LaVeris)
"When things get taken away, and if that's everything – your fame and your attachment to this stuff – if that gets taken from you, and that's all you have, then you have nothing," he said.
"But if you realize there is something higher than all of that and your connection to that, then at that point there's nothing that anybody could do to you."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

He added, "The thing about Christianity, it's really … it's love others, and it's really about forgiveness. And forgiveness isn't something you give to somebody else. It's a gift you give to yourself. You can't carry stuff. You have to let go."
King's representatives did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Tracy Wright is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital. Send story tips to Tracy.Wright@fox.com.

title: ‘X-Files’ star Gillian Anderson reveals parenting regret, says she wishes she was 'less selfish'
summary: Gillian Anderson reveals she wishes she'd been "less selfish" in early parenting while filming "The X-Files" and working grueling 17-hour days.
story: "Chrisley Knows Best" stars Todd and Julie Chrisley explained how their approaches to parenting changed since their time in prison.
Gillian Anderson is looking back at the sacrifices she made as her Hollywood career took off — and acknowledging that some of those choices came at a cost for her family.

In a new interview with The Sunday Times, the 58-year-old actress — who became a household name playing FBI Special Agent Dana Scully on "The X-Files" — opened up about her regrets as a young mother and explained how the show’s grueling production schedule affected her ability to be present for her daughter.

"I have absolutely no regrets in my life," Anderson initially told the outlet before reconsidering. "No, there are a couple of things, in terms of early parenting, that I now would say, I wish I’d thought this through or I wish I’d been less selfish."
SCARLETT JOHANSSON, WHO EARNED $43 MILLION IN 2025, SAYS LIFE IS A CONSTANT 'DEFICIT' AT HOME
Gillian Anderson said she regrets working so much when her daughter was a young child. (Getty Images)
Anderson became a mother at 26, welcoming daughter Piper with her first husband, "The X-Files" assistant art director Clyde Klotz, just over a year after she began filming the hit Fox sci-fi series.
Her career was rapidly accelerating at the time, with "The X-Files" becoming a global phenomenon and Anderson facing grueling days on set.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
After Anderson and Klotz divorced in 1997, Piper split her time between her mother, who was working on "The X-Files" in Los Angeles, and her father in Vancouver.
OLIVIA WILDE SPEAKS OUT ABOUT THE EXACT MOMENT SHE KNEW RELATIONSHIP WITH JASON SUDEIKIS WAS OVER

In an effort to maintain consistency in her daughter's education, Piper attended a French lycée in both cities. The arrangement, however, meant the young girl was regularly traveling between her parents.
Anderson is mom to three children. (Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images)
"It was intense for her, with no French in the household, to suddenly be getting a plane every three weeks," Anderson recalled. "It’s a lot to ask of a six-year-old."

The actress said she was working 17-hour days and didn't believe she was in a position to push back against the demanding schedule, despite being one of the show's two central stars alongside David Duchovny.
TOM SELLECK SAYS 'BLUE BLOODS' CAST MADE MAJOR SACRIFICE TO SAVE SHOW BEFORE CANCELLATION
"That show couldn’t have done without [me], and so I had leverage that I’m not sure I knew," Anderson said.
Anderson has previously spoken about wondering whether she could have made different choices as a working mother.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

In a previous interview with The Sunday Times, the actress acknowledged there was another version of her life in which she could have worked less, lived on a smaller scale and been more present for her children.
Gillian Anderson starred as FBI Special Agent Dana Scully on "The X-Files" opposite David Duchovny, who played FBI Special Agent Fox Mulder, from 1993 to 2002. (Getty Images)

"There's another version of my life where I could have worked less, had a smaller life and been more present as a parent. I could have chosen that, that could happen," she said. "But sometimes it feels like why would you, if you keep getting work as an actor, doing things you dreamt of doing and being offered incredible roles at this age, while paying the bills, and you still get to see them a huge percentage of the time and they witness a mother enjoying her work?
Her approach to parenting changed when she later welcomed sons Oscar and Felix with businessman Mark Griffiths.
GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'
Despite reflecting on what she might have done differently, Anderson has continued working steadily decades after "The X-Files" made her famous.
The actress turned 58 on Aug. 9. (Getty Images)
HEATHER GRAHAM SAYS CLASSMATES DISMISSED HER AS 'NERDY' BEFORE HOLLYWOOD BREAKTHROUGH PROVED THEM WRONG

Her more recent credits include "The Crown," "Sex Education" and "The Salt Path." She also stars opposite Hannah Einbinder in filmmaker Jane Schoenbrun’s "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma," which premiered at the Cannes Film Festival.
Anderson suggested that her relationship with work remains complicated as she approaches 60.
"I feel very lucky to still be working," she told The Sunday Times, adding that while she once imagined slowing down in her 60s to direct and make art, she is reconsidering those plans.

"I’m having so much fun," she said.

title: Chrissy Metz slams weight loss critics, says they're always 'going to have something to say'
summary: Chrissy Metz slams online critics commenting on her body and reveals how her father's death from obesity complications led her to start GLP-1 medication.
story: Chrissy Metz tells Fox News Digital she was the middle child of five.
Chrissy Metz is firing back at the haters commenting on her weight loss.
During a recent appearance on "The Tamsen Show" podcast, the 45-year-old actress spoke about why she chose to start taking a GLP-1 medication and slammed haters who comment on her body.

"It's not that I don't have people and naysayers and people who comment all kinds of stuff still to this day," she said. "Like I don't know when people will stop doing that. I don't think it ever will happen."
She then recalled a recent incident in which a distant relative congratulated her for "taking control of your weight," as "weight has always been an issue in our family."
Metz shared internet trolls will always have something to say. (Raymond Hall/GC Images)
JACK OSBOURNE FIRES BACK AT BODY SHAMERS CALLING HIM 'GROSSLY UNDERWEIGHT'

Metz explained that the relative is "an overweight woman" herself, so she understands the struggles of living in the world as an overweight person. She said comments about her weight from the relative don't sting as much, but added, "The other comments are a little…it's wild to me."

"It's interesting what people say cause would they ever say it to you on the streets? Never. Never," she explained. "They're like, 'Oh, Chrissy, you're pretty, but them eyebrows.' I'm like, 'Oh my god, it doesn't matter what I do. It doesn't matter.'"
She then shared some of the types of comments she received, including "Why'd you wear that? Why did you do this? Like why aren't you losing weight? Oh, you're losing weight?"

"It doesn't matter. It doesn't matter what you do," Metz said. "And I know it's not personal, but it can be taxing, but you sometimes just got to just shut it off cuz no matter what you do, somebody's going to have something to say."
Metz is currently starring in the Broadway musical, "& Juliet." (Getty Images for A+E Global Media)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Metz, who is currently starring in the Broadway musical "& Juliet," called receiving all the criticism and "still doing what you want to do...an act of rebellion."
The "This Is Us" actress also discussed her use of a GLP-1 medication this week during an appearance on "Today."

She told the podcast host that she was always "skeptical" of GLP-1s and that it was something she "was so afraid of even sort of partaking in," but her mentality changed when her father "unfortunately passed away from obesity complications."
One of the ways in which the medication helped her was by quieting the food noise in her mind, which she described as being "loud."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Metz said the GLP-1 has helped her quiet the food noise. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"I know it sounds so silly now, but I'm like, 'Oh, not everybody hears that all the time? Oh, okay. Oh, there's like something chemically off and metabolically off and hereditary, you know, issues,'" she said. "And so really when that happened with my family and my father, I was like, I have to do something about it. And so, yeah...I feel better on the medication."
The actress is now partnering with Ro, a telehealth company that provides medications for a number of issues, including weight loss.

title: Kelly Clarkson won’t let her kids watch ‘From Justin to Kelly’ after brutal admission about 2003 film
summary: Kelly Clarkson revealed at her final Las Vegas concert that she has banned her children from watching "From Justin to Kelly," calling it bluntly terrible.
story: Kate Hudson told Fox News Digital that she is actively trying not to raise fame-obsessed children.
Kelly Clarkson has no plans to introduce her children to one infamous chapter of her career.

During her final Las Vegas concert on Saturday, the 44-year-old singer revealed that she has banned daughter River Rose, 12, and son Remington, 10, from watching her 2003 musical comedy, "From Justin to Kelly."

"Well, it’s an Oscar-worthy number, and it’s called ‘From Justin to Kelly,’" Clarkson joked, according to a video obtained by Us Weekly, before explaining her participation in two words: "Contractually obligated."
KELLY CLARKSON LAUGHS OFF WIND-BLOWN WARDROBE MALFUNCTION ON STAGE
Kelly Clarkson and Justin Guarini co-starred in the 2003 musical comedy, "From Justin to Kelly." (Getty Images)

"Man, read the f—ing fine print, you know," she told the crowd. "I didn’t know that if you won, you had to do a movie. Not all of us want to be Meryl Streep, we just like watching her, OK? I was like, ‘I don’t want to be in a movie,’ but they were like, ‘Yeah, but you won.’ And I was like, ‘And I feel like I’m losing? It doesn’t feel quite like a win.’"
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Clarkson starred opposite "American Idol" season one runner-up Justin Guarini in the musical, which hit theaters shortly after she became the reality competition’s inaugural winner. The movie followed two young people who meet and fall for each other while on spring break.
Clarkson, who won the first season of "American Idol," said the movie she made with runner-up Guarini was "s---." (SGranitz/WireImage/Getty Images)
More than two decades later, Clarkson made clear she isn't looking back at the project through rose-colored glasses.
After a fan at the concert defended the film, Clarkson joked that the audience member was watching it with "loving eyes," before offering her own decidedly less flattering assessment: "It’s s---."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
And her two children apparently won't get the chance to judge her performance for themselves anytime soon.
"It is funny though, like, my kids, I’ve banned them from watching," Clarkson admitted.
Clarkson said she was "contractually obligated" to make the film after winning the first season. (Kevin Winter/ImageDirect)
Despite her feelings about the film, the singer said the experience wasn't entirely negative.
"The music part, that was fun," she said. "See? You gotta find the positive, motherf—ers, you know? Turn that s— into lemonade … and cry yourself to sleep."

"From Justin to Kelly" was released in 2003, one year after Clarkson's victory on the first season of "American Idol."

title: ‘American Pie’ star Shannon Elizabeth swears off dating, says OnlyFans is ‘the only relationship I need’
summary: Shannon Elizabeth told Bill Maher on "Club Random" that OnlyFans is "the only relationship I need" after swearing off dating following her divorce.
story: Shannon Elizabeth opens up about joining OnlyFans, exploring boundaries and finding empowerment during a major life transition.
Shannon Elizabeth isn’t looking for another slice of romance anytime soon.
The "American Pie" star, whose divorce was finalized in May, has sworn off dating, insisting that OnlyFans is "the only relationship I need."
During an appearance on Bill Maher's "Club Random" podcast, he asked her, "What’s the dating scene like in Cape Town?" Elizabeth moved to South Africa in 2016 to focus on wildlife conservation.
‘AMERICAN PIE’ ALUM SHANNON ELIZABETH TURNS TO ONLYFANS FOR ‘FRESH START’ AS DIVORCE UNFOLDS
In May, actress Shannon Elizabeth spoke to Fox News Digital about her decision to join OnlyFans and how fun it's been for her. (Jonathan Leibson/Getty Images for Patron)
"I'm very newly single, and I don’t plan on ever dating again, to be honest," Elizabeth replied.
"Come on, you’re going to date," Maher insisted.
"No, no," Elizabeth said.
"No, not even dating?" Maher said.
WATCH: ‘AMERICAN PIE’ STAR LAUNCHES ONLYFANS, EMBRACES FRESH START
"I do not want to date," Elizabeth said. "I’m not interested. There’s too many con artists out there. There’s too many people I don’t trust. I have no interest."
"... The only relationships I need are the relationships on OnlyFans that I’m building with all of these people," Elizabeth said.
Maher was adamant that Elizabeth’s ban on dating wouldn’t stick.
Comedian and television host Bill Maher spoke to Shannon Elizabeth on his podcast "Club Random with Bill Maher." (Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images)
"Well, I’m not saying I know you better than you, because I don’t," he said. "You know you better than you. I will say this: I have heard that from many people right after. ..."
"I mean, including many celebrities," he said.

Maher pointed to Halle Berry as an example, noting that the actress had once said she would never marry again. Berry later married actor Olivier Martinez in 2013, and the couple filed for divorce in 2015.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Halle Berry and Olivier Martinez married on July 13, 2013, in France. They announced their separation and filed for divorce in October 2015. They were declared legally single in December 2016, and their divorce settlement was finalized in August 2023. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)
Elizabeth wasn't swayed.
"... At the moment, I’m perfectly fine not being with anyone and not wanting anything," she said.

OnlyFans allows creators to charge fans directly for their content, and Elizabeth found immediate financial success on the subscription platform. Variety reported that she earned more than $1.2 million in her first week after launching her account in April.
Shannon Elizabeth is interviewed by Jay Leno on "The Tonight Show" on Aug. 23, 2001. (Paul Drinkwater/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal)

For Elizabeth, however, OnlyFans has become more than another source of income. She told Variety the platform provided a financial lifeline as she went through her divorce from Simon Borchert. Acting roles weren't coming in as frequently as they once did, she said, and she had largely been living off her savings.

"For the last ten years, I’ve been living off of my savings for the most part, because I haven’t been as focused on work," she said. "To be able to get myself back to the point where I’m not struggling and am able to choose projects because I like them and not because I need the money — it’s definitely giving me more freedom to do that."
WATCH: SHANNON ELIZABETH REFLECTS ON ‘AMERICAN PIE’ AND NEW MISSION
Elizabeth also wants to direct and "be behind the camera." In the meantime, she’s directing and producing her OnlyFans content, which does not currently include nudity.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Shannon Elizabeth, who starred in 1999's "American Pie," has moved to South Africa where she launched the Shannon Elizabeth Foundation to help wildlife in need. (Cliff Lipson/CBS via Getty Images)

"I’ve got to be a little bit mysterious," she said. "I do all kinds of content, but I don’t even know what my boundaries will be. I’m still exploring it, and as I become more comfortable with it, I’m going to push those boundaries."
A portion of Elizabeth’s OnlyFans earnings goes to her wildlife conservation nonprofit.
Elizabeth previously told Fox News Digital that she isn't worried about criticism of her latest venture.
Shannon Elizabeth played Nadia, Jim’s foreign exchange student crush, in "American Pie" (1999). (Getty Images)

"I know people do make assumptions about creators on the platform," she said. "But I don’t go looking for it. And people have been nothing but really supportive and kind to me. ... I’m really happy doing it. I’m really having so much fun. I’m connecting with people. And I think no matter what you do in any industry, there’s always going to be people who don’t support you, who want to bring you down or who criticize you."
One piece of advice Elizabeth would give to another actress considering OnlyFans is simple: Just do it.

"Absolutely do it," she gushed. "It’s been an incredible experience. And if you don’t like it, you just stop. That’s the beauty of it. The control’s in your hands. So if you want to do it for one month, do it for a month. See if you like it. In fact, I have already started talking to some friends about getting on the platform with me, and a lot of people are starting to consider it."
Shannon Elizabeth at the 33rd Annual EMA Awards Gala held at Sunset Las Palmas Studios on Jan. 27, 2024, in Los Angeles. (Christopher Polk/Variety via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"[This is] something that we wanted to do 25 years ago, but the technology wasn’t there yet," she said. "Now the technology is there. I just wish I’d done it sooner."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Amanda Kloots confronts biggest misconception about dating after losing a spouse
summary: Amanda Kloots tells Fox News Digital dating after losing Nick Cordero to COVID-19 doesn't mean loving him any less, revealing the misconception widows face most.
story: The "Good Grief" podcast host tells Fox News Digital losing a spouse doesn't close the door to love, sharing why widows and widowers can embrace new relationships.
Amanda Kloots is challenging a common misconception about dating after losing a spouse — that moving forward means leaving the person you lost behind.

Kloots, who lost her husband, Broadway star Nick Cordero, to COVID-19 in 2020, said widows and widowers can face judgment when they begin opening their hearts to someone new — even though grief and love don't simply disappear when a new relationship begins.
AMANDA KLOOTS HONORS LATE HUSBAND NICK CORDERO IN NEW MEMOIR, SAYS HE ‘TRULY JUST LOVED LIFE’
Amanda Kloots opens up about feeling spiritually connected to Nick Cordero six years after his death while embracing new love and relationships. (Jason Armond/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

"The heart can hold a lot of love," Kloots said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "And just because I'm dating again or any widow or widower is dating again, it doesn't mean that you don't love your person that you lost still or any less."
"It’s in fact more," the "Good Grief" podcast host shared.
Kloots isn't asking people to believe that grief disappears.
She's asking them to acknowledge that it doesn't have to prevent someone from living.
AMANDA KLOOTS SHARES 'HUGE MEDICAL BILL' FROM NICK CORDERO'S HOSPITAL STAY, VENTILATOR COST $3,000 DAILY
The "Good Grief" podcast host shares how her heart holds space for Nick Cordero and new love, urging people to support widows. (Phillip Faraone/Getty Images)

"I have many compartments in my heart for love and new relationships," she said. "It's like having more children. It doesn't mean you… love your child less… now [that] you have a new child. Your heart is able to hold many, many types of love, and I wish people understood that you can hold those two things very close."
She said new love does not erase old love.
And for anyone who dates a widow or widower, Kloots explained that reality needs to be understood from the start.
WATCH: AMANDA KLOOTS DEFENDS DATING AGAIN AFTER HUSBAND NICK CORDERO'S DEATH
"These people are never leaving our lives, but there's definitely room and space for new love, new relationships, new marriage and it's so beautiful."
"Celebrate and help and support friends in your life who are on this journey," she said. "It is so difficult and it is so hard and if you make it harder for us, it really isn't fair."
Amanda Kloots challenges the misconception about widows dating, saying grief and new love can coexist. (Jim Spellman/WireImage)

"So really support those people and guide them along on this because they're doing something that is something they never wish they had to do," she continued. "It's not, they're not dating again because ‘yay!’ It's a different type of dating again. So, support them, love them, be kind."

Cordero died on July 5, 2020, after spending 95 days in the hospital battling COVID-19. The Broadway star endured mini-strokes, blood clots, septic infections and a tracheostomy before doctors amputated his right leg.

Kloots documented his fight for his life publicly, giving followers a front-row seat to a nightmare that began just as she, Cordero and their then-9-month-old son, Elvis, were starting a new life in Los Angeles.
They had moved from New York City in March 2020, chasing what was supposed to be a dream.
Kloots suddenly became a widow — and she's never stopped talking about Cordero.
WATCH: AMANDA KLOOTS SHARES HOW SHE STILL FEELS LATE HUSBAND NICK CORDERO'S PRESENCE
She believes stopping the conversation is one of the biggest mistakes people make after someone dies.

"If he was still alive, I'd be talking about him all the time. He's still in my life. I have a son that I'm raising that's his, and I need to make sure that Elvis knows who his dad was and that the world never forgets him."
Cordero, she said, "was such a beautiful man."
Amanda Kloots urges others to keep talking about their loved ones after they're gone. (Walter McBride/WireImage)

"And I don't think anyone we lose has to be forgotten forever," she continued. "Keep saying their names, keep talking about them, keep celebrating them, celebrate their birthdays, celebrate their anniversaries, honor them at the holidays, and every day. They can still be around."
For Kloots, Cordero's presence isn't simply a metaphor. She says she has continued to feel spiritually connected to him since his death.
"You know, they mean everything," Kloots said of the signs she believes she receives from him.

"I feel like when you lose somebody there's such a finality with death, and you really feel like there's no way you'll ever connect with them again, of course. And I started asking for signs right away from Nick, and he started showing up and I just kind of really went all in on it..."
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I do feel like he's around Elvis and I all the time, and we get signs all the time from him, and I feel like he's on my spirit team just guiding us every single day, and I do feel this really beautiful spiritual connection with him that has got me through these last six years."
Amanda Kloots in episode 101 of Netflix's "Let's Marry Harry." (Netflix)
That perspective has followed Kloots into her newest chapter — including her role on Netflix's "Let's Marry Harry."
The show puts reality star and notorious bachelor Harry Jowsey's dating life in the hands of three trusted friends, with Kloots serving as a big-sister-like confidante.
WATCH: AMANDA KLOOTS AND REALITY STAR HARRY JOWSEY TOOK 'FULL INVENTORY' OF HIS DATING LIFE BEFORE 'LET'S MARRY HARRY'
Before filming began, she and Jowsey spent time talking about love, marriage and relationships.
"I told him constantly, you know, how you love is so important and marriage changes over time. And you have to really love and communicate with your partner."
Amanda Kloots officiated Harry Jowsey's wedding on the Netflix show. (Netflix)
Kloots said she quickly noticed a pattern in Jowsey's romantic history.
"He had kind of a track record of fighting equaled love for him."
She challenged him to rethink it.
"What if we flip the switch here? Because I've learned, you know, that I shouldn't have fought so much with my partner. I would take them all back now. I don't have him around anymore."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Kloots emphasized to Fox News Digital that she isn’t romanticizing loss but learning from it.
Amanda Kloots launched her podcast "Good Grief with Amanda Kloots." (Amanda Kloots)
She's turning that experience into "Good Grief with Amanda Kloots," her new podcast.
The show tackles grief in its many forms, from death and divorce to lost careers, relationships, identities and futures people thought they were guaranteed to have.
Kloots' grief doesn't have an expiration date, and neither does love.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Six years after Cordero's death, she is still carrying him with her while making room for the life ahead.
Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: What Taylor Sheridan's biggest stars really think about working with the 'Yellowstone' creator
summary: Zoe Saldaña, Billy Bob Thornton, Harrison Ford and Kevin Costner reveal what it's really like working with Taylor Sheridan on his hit shows.
story: Billy Bob Thornton told Fox News Digital that Taylor Sheridan's "Landman" is a worldwide phenomenon.
The third season of Taylor Sheridan's hit show "Lioness" has officially begun.

"Lioness" is one of many successful shows created by the prolific TV writer and showrunner. His long list of credits also include "Yellowstone," "1923," "Landman," "The Madison" and many other popular shows.
It's not only audiences who have fallen in love with the complex characters and storylines Sheridan has created, but also the actors who work on his sets.
Here is what some of his stars have said about what it's really like to work with Sheridan.
ZOE SALDANA SAYS TAYLOR SHERIDAN GIVES STARS TWO CHOICES: 'MAKE SURE THAT YOU DON'T F--K UP... OR YOU QUIT'
Sheridan's actors have all spoken about his abilities as a writer. (Omar Vega/Getty Images)
Michael Kelly
Kelly called Sheridan "one of the greatest storytellers in history." (TheStewartofNY/FilmMagic)
Ahead of the season three premiere of "Lioness," one of its stars, Michael Kelly, told People that Sheridan is "truly a standalone talent."
"There’s nobody who’s doing or has ever done what he’s doing," he said. "It’s incredible what he does. And he’s just one of the smartest dudes you’ll ever meet."
He added, "He’s f---ing brilliant, man. Brilliant. And just one of the greatest storytellers."

When it comes to working with the showrunner in the future, Kelly said that while he's "never thought about how the shows could cross over," he has told Sheridan, "anything you want me to do, I'll do."
He told Sheridan, "I love being in Texas. I love saying your words," and, "Anything, dude. You can put me in. Put me in, coach. Wherever you want to put me, I’ll go."
Zoe Saldaña

Zoe Saldaña opened up about working with Taylor Sheridan, saying the "Lioness" creator challenges actors while remaining collaborative on set. (Dia Dipasupil/WireImage/Getty Images; Phillip Faraone/Getty Images for Viacom/Getty Images)

Actress Zoe Saldaña has starred in all three seasons of "Lioness," and told "CBS Mornings" that while she can "feel like an old soldier" on set, when Sheridan shows he believes in her, "you have no other choice but to start believing in yourself again."
The actress also referred to him as "an intimidating cat," who comes to set ready and "so serious," noting, "it raises the bar for the rest of us."

"So working with him is a challenge in the sense that he does raise the bar," Saldaña also told People. "And you have one of two choices. You either accept the challenge and make sure that you don't f--- up... or you quit."
Zoe Saldaña plays the role of Joe in "Lioness." (Lauren Smith/Paramount+)

She added that one of the benefits of working with Sheridan is that "he's an incredibly smart person" who puts in a ton of research when writing his scripts, "And then he writes these incredibly elaborate shows that end up really educating us as well."
"It's actually great," she added. "When you work with him is when you realize how passionate he is about actors and about acting. I think it is his first love when it comes to the arts."
Billy Bob Thornton
Thornton said he loves working with Sheridan on "Landman." (Scott Dudelson/Getty Images for Stagecoach)
When speaking at a Q&A in Hollywood in April, "Landman" star Billy Bob Thornton told the crowd that he has a lot of trust in the show, noting, "I trust Taylor and I trust the castmates."
"Yeah, oh, it’s great. I love working with Taylor," Thornton said, per People. "I love hanging out with him after hours. He’s such a brilliant guy, great writer, and I love his company."
Michelle Pfeiffer
Pfeiffer checked with Helen Mirren before accepting the role in Sheridan's show, "The Madison." (Steve Granitz/FilmMagic)
When speaking with The Hollywood Reporter in March, Michelle Pfeiffer spoke about how Sheridan convinced her to star in "The Madison."

"[Taylor] wanted to know who Stacy was before he started writing. I wanted to know who Stacy is before I committed. And so we went back and forth like that for a little while, and it became clear to me I wasn’t going to win this battle," Pfeiffer said. "So I asked Helen Mirren [who previously starred in Sheridan's "Yellowstone" spinoff "1923"] to speak to me about her experience."

"And she just glowed; she couldn’t say enough nice things," Pfeiffer recalled of Mirren. "She said the scripts were great, the productions were perfect. She was having the time of her life; she loved Montana. So I took a big leap of faith, and I committed. I thought, 'Well, the guy has a pretty darn good track record.'"
Harrison Ford
Ford called Sheridan an incredible writer and an intellectual. (John Sciulli/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images)

Harrison Ford starred in Sheridan's "Yellowstone" prequel series, "1923," and had nothing but nice things to say about the showrunner when speaking about him at the premiere of the show in December 2022.
"He’s an incredible horseman. He’s a genuine athlete, and that’s something you might not expect to find in such a talented writer and intellectual thinker," he told The Hollywood Reporter.
Kevin Costner
Costner told Entertainment Weekly that Sheridan is "doing special work." (Getty Images)

Ahead of the release of his movie "Horizon: An American Saga" in 2024, Kevin Costner spoke with Entertainment Weekly about working with Sheridan, as his future on "Yellowstone" was uncertain at the time.
The actor told the outlet that Sheridan is "doing special work in a lot of different ways."

"He's very prolific about the things he does, and if he sees me in something that he wants to do, I'll look at it just the way I did 'Yellowstone' and maybe we will end up doing something together," Costner says. "He likes a lot of the things that I like, and the idea of us working together is not out of the question for me."

He went on to say that "the subjects he chooses are very interesting to me," and that, aside from "Yellowstone," "other things that he's doing, I think, are really, really good. He likes the same subjects that I do."
Costner ultimately didn't return to film the last episodes of "Yellowstone." (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Airbnb)

Costner ultimately did not return to film the remainder of "Yellowstone" season five. A new spinoff, "Dutton Ranch," continued the Dutton family's story and followed Cole Hauser and Kelly Reilly's characters as they left Montana to start a new life in Texas.
Helen Mirren
Mirren starred in the "Yellowstone" spinoff series "1923." (Karwai Tang/WireImage; Emerson Miller/Paramount+)
Helen Mirren spoke to The Hollywood Reporter in December 2022 at the premiere of "1923."
When speaking with the outlet, she gave fans an inside look at what it's like working with Sheridan, calling him "fabulously hands-off."

"He presents the script, and it’s so extraordinary that you don’t want to change a word. You want to do it exactly as it’s written because it’s written with incredible precision but without being labored," she said. "To be able to be a part of a franchise in a world that is so singular on American television is very exciting. There’s nothing else quite like it."
Brian Geraghty
Geraghty praised Sheraton for his writing and casting ability. (Valerie Terranova/Getty Images for Searchlight Pictures)
"1923" star Brian Geraghty spoke with The Hollywood Reporter at the premiere of the show in December 2022 about his experience working with Sheridan.
Geraghty explained that he "expected someone totally different" prior to meeting Sheridan for the first time, and how his experience as an actor makes him a great showrunner.
'LANDMAN' STAR MICHELLE RANDOLPH STUNS IN BARELY-THERE METALLIC YELLOW BIKINI IN NEW SUMMER PHOTO DUMP

"He told me great stories of his time as an actor, about the process and how he hired some of the younger actors on the show by giving them a break over some really big-name actors," he said. "I love that because we all need that break. I got it 15 or 20 years ago and a few of the actors on the show got that from him."
He explained that his experience as an actor makes him "really empathetic to actor," although he presents as "this tough cowboy."
Geraghty starred in the "Yellowstone" spinoff, "1923." (Rodin Eckenroth/WireImage)

"I think he casts really well, and he does not care what you have done, for the most part. He casts the people who are right for the role," he explained. "When you show up to work, everyone raises the bar. He creates that, and it starts from him, but he also is very welcoming and gives you the tools you need to get there."
Michelle Randolph
Michelle Randolph played Elizabeth Strafford in "1923." (James Minchin III/Paramount+)
Michelle Randolph, who has appeared in both "1923" and "Landman," echoed Geraghty's statement and credited Sheridan for being willing to give unknown actors a break.

When speaking to People in 2025, Randolph praised Sheridan as "one of the few people" in the business who "takes chances on actors" and who "has given us this opportunity, and I just am eternally grateful for him."
"He made my dreams come true. I tell him that every time I see him," Randolph said. "He's like, 'Michelle, stop. I get it.' I'm like, 'Thank you.' But he really did give us something."

In addition to praising his casting methods, Randolph also complimented him as a writer, telling The Hollywood Reporter in December 2022 that he gives his characters "such depth and such unique storylines."
Randolph credits Sheridan for changing her life by taking a chance on her as an actress. (Gilbert Flores/WWD via Getty Images)

"No matter how many different situations are going on at once," she said. "Every character is so uniquely themselves and that’s really hard to do as a writer, especially for the amount of shows that he’s writing for."
Kurt Russell
Russell said "The Madison" is Sheridan's best writing. (Gilbert Flores/Variety via Getty Images)
Kurt Russell could not help but praise Sheridan's writing ability while at the premiere of "The Madison" in March.

"I love his writing. I think this is his best writing. I love that this is not 'Yellowstone.' It's not that. It's very, it's very standalone, very different," he told Page Six. "I love the relationships that he digs into here. And I think that this is truly a different wheelhouse for him. It was fun to do."

Ali Larter
Larter, who plays Angela in "Landman," revealed she knew Sheridan prior to being cast on the show but hadn't spoken to him in a decade. (Emerson Miller/Paramount+)
Ali Larter has developed a close friendship with Sheridan through working with him on "Landman."
When speaking with People in April, Larter shared that Sheridan will often text her as he is writing, saying "if he’s laughing at his own writing… I’ll get a text."

"I mean, you know, the first season, I spent a ton of time with Taylor," she said. "He has a very clear vision of what he wants… and he is a visionary because when he is writing the scripts, he knows how he’s going to edit them."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
She went on to say that, as actors, they often "want to advocate for your character," but Sheridan is "brilliant" at creating a world "where that fits into the story that he wants to tell."
Larter credited Sheridan for being an amazing writer. (Emerson Miller/Paramount+)
Larter also praised his writing ability and work ethic when speaking with Taste of Country, calling him "the best working writer."
"He's brilliant at the way he crafts his stories," she said. "I love the characters he creates, because they're dynamic and powerful ... But he also has space to show their vulnerable sides."
When speaking with The Hollywood Reporter in June, Larter shared that she and Sheridan knew one another before "Landman," but that they hadn't spoken in over a decade when she was cast on the show.
Larter called Sheridan "an extraordinarily hard worker." (GC Images)

"I don’t think that you can pin him down," she told the outlet. "I think that he’s not going to come back into the machine that just wants to break him down. And he wants to work. He’s an extraordinarily hard worker. He’s a brilliant talent. He wants to do it his way. And I think that it’s very hard in our industry to do things your own way when you’re part of the machine."

title: Jessica Simpson turns heads in bikini photos from trip to Turks and Caicos
summary: Jessica Simpson shared bikini photos from her Turks and Caicos birthday trip on Instagram, lounging in a black polka dot two-piece in paradise.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Among the photos included in the post is a black-and-white picture of the "With You" singer smiling as she posed for a selfie while lying on a lounge chair in a black bikini with small white polka dots.
She paired the bikini with a pair of black sunglasses and a necklace which went down the center of her chest.
Simpson shared a bikini photo from her vacation to Turks and Caicos. (Jessica Simpson Instagram)
JULIANNE HOUGH FLAUNTS HER TONED FIGURE IN BIKINIS AS SHE SHARES SNAPS FROM HER TRIP TO SARDINIA
"Take me back to Turks and Caicos," she captioned the post. "Thank you @lacurevillas and @pavilionluxuryvillas for an unforgettable stay. We’ll be seein’ y’all again very very soon."

Simpson also shared photos of her in a black dress and one of her in a black cover-up standing next to the ocean. (Jessica Simpson Instagram)

The singer previously shared a photo of herself in a separate black-and-white polka-dot bikini on her birthday in July, captioning the post, "46 July 10/26."
Simpson celebrated eight years of sobriety in November 2025. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for JS)

'BAYWATCH: HAWAII' STAR BRANDY LEDFORD SAYS SHE 'WANTED TO TRULY CHECK OUT' BEFORE REHAB SAVED HER LIFE
"I’m so happy I chose faith over fear," she added. "It was not in the fight that I found my strength, it was in the surrender."
Simpson previously shared she stopped drinking the day after Halloween in 2017. (Aeon/GC Images)

title: Cancer risk may be higher for people with one particular type of job
summary: A Harvard study found U.S. pilots and flight attendants face the highest radiation-related cancer mortality risk out of more than 500 occupations.
story: Flight attendants and pilots in the U.S. face the highest risk of radiation-related cancer deaths out of a list of more than 500 occupations, study author Anupam B. Jena told Fox News Digital.
People who fly for a living could face a higher risk of certain types of cancers, a new Harvard study suggests.
Flight attendants and pilots in the U.S. face the highest risk of radiation-related cancer deaths out of a list of more than 500 occupations, the researchers concluded.
"As you get high up in the atmosphere, you're exposed to ionizing radiation from the sun. It's called cosmic radiation," study author Anupam B. Jena, M.D., Ph.D., told Fox News Digital.
CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’

The finding was based on analysis of data from the National Vital Statistics System, specifically, nearly 13 million U.S. death certificates between 2020 and 2024. Out of those records, 14,000 were pilots and 7,000 were flight attendants.
People who fly for a living could face a higher risk of certain types of cancers, a new Harvard study suggests. (iStock)

Across all occupations, the team analyzed mortality from radiation-related cancers, including breast cancer, multiple myeloma, leukemia (except chronic lymphocytic leukemia), lymphoma, central nervous system cancers, thyroid cancer, prostate cancer, melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancers.
They did not include lung cancer to prevent confounding the results with any smoking-related risk.
CANCER WARNING SIGNS MAY APPEAR IN DNA YEARS BEFORE BLOOD TESTS DETECT TROUBLE

Pilots and flight attendants were found to have "statistically significantly" higher mortality rates linked to breast cancer, central nervous system cancers, prostate cancers and melanoma. Pilots were also more likely to die from leukemia.
Among all flight attendant deaths, 6.9% were linked to radiation-related cancers, as were 6.7% of pilots’ deaths. This was higher than the rates for any other occupations, the researchers found.
Flight attendants and pilots in the U.S. face the highest risk of radiation-related cancer deaths out of a list of more than 500 occupations, the researchers concluded. (iStock)
For cancers not related to radiation, the rates were comparable to other occupations.
"It's not just lifestyle factors or factors about these individuals that are making them more likely to develop cancer at large," Jena added.
The study was published Aug. 17 in JAMA Internal Medicine.
"Just making sure that these individuals are screened regularly, that they may be screened earlier in life than other folks — I think that's totally on the table."
"The risk increase is meaningful enough for the group," Jena said. "Our study doesn't speak to the individual pilot or flight attendant, but more so to the two groups as a whole."

Each year, airline workers receive about 3 to 6 millisieverts of cosmic radiation, compared to 0.4 millisieverts for someone who takes 10 round-trip cross-country flights, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
That means airline workers may receive roughly eight to 15 times the annual cosmic radiation exposure of someone taking 10 cross-country round trips.
"It is thought that this would be a cumulative risk, so the more time that you're exposed to that cosmic radiation, the greater the increase in risk that you might experience," Jena pointed out.
The findings could raise questions about whether U.S. pilots and flight attendants should receive additional or earlier cancer screenings. (iStock)
The findings could also raise questions about whether U.S. pilots and flight attendants should receive additional or earlier cancer screenings.
"I think the level of screening may need to be higher," Jena said, noting that approaches differ between the U.S. and other countries.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Just making sure that these individuals are screened regularly, that they may be screened earlier in life than other folks — I think that's totally on the table."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

For people who fly frequently for business or pleasure, Jena said the findings should be less concerning, noting that very few passengers accumulate flight time comparable to pilots and flight attendants.
He added, "This is really sort of a consideration for people who spend their life in the air."
The researchers did not have access to data on individual workers’ radiation exposure, which means they could not determine whether those with greater exposure faced greater risks. (iStock)

The study has several limitations. Because it was observational, the findings cannot establish that cosmic radiation caused the elevated cancer mortality among pilots and flight attendants, only that the two were associated.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The researchers also did not have access to data on individual workers’ radiation exposure, which means they could not determine whether those with greater exposure faced greater risks.
Other occupational or lifestyle factors could also potentially contribute to the findings.

title: Parkinson’s patient’s yearslong tremor vanishes within minutes of new ultrasound treatment
summary: Bud Leavell's Parkinson's tremor vanished minutes after receiving FDA-approved focused ultrasound at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Arlington, Texas.
story: Dr. Bhavya Shah, a neuroradiologist at UT Southwestern Medical Center, discusses a focused ultrasound treatment that was approved by the FDA in January 2026 to treat the primary motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease, including stiffness and slowness.
Bud Leavell, 72, suffered from severe tremors for years after his Parkinson's diagnosis, making it impossible for him to enjoy his favorite pastime of repairing radios in his garage.
But within minutes of receiving a newly approved ultrasound treatment, his tremor was completely gone.
Leavell, a retired salesman and Air Force veteran in Arlington, Texas, experienced the dramatic before-and-after result at UT Southwestern Medical Center.
CARLY SIMON REVEALS THE COMMON CONDITION THAT MASKED HER PARKINSON'S DIAGNOSIS
The focused ultrasound targeted precise areas deep in Leavell’s brain. Unlike deep brain stimulation, which requires opening the skull, this new treatment is non-invasive.

At his latest follow-up, Leavell's tremor remained as well-controlled as it was immediately after the procedure, according to his doctor. When asked how the tremor was doing, Leavell responded with, "What tremor?"
A non-invasive approach
Leavell was diagnosed with Parkinson’s in 2017, immediately following surgery for thyroid cancer.
"My voice was weak and gravelly, and within a few days, a tremor set into my right hand," he shared with Fox News Digital. "Before this time, I was experiencing a slow loss of my sense of smell."

The tremors made it "frustratingly difficult" for Leavell to perform certain functions, especially anything that required fine motor skills in his dominant hand, such as using his binoculars or clicking a computer mouse.
NEUROLOGIST REVEALS WHY PARKINSON'S SYMPTOMS ARE OFTEN MISTAKEN FOR OTHER CONDITIONS

Dr. Bhavya Shah, a neuroradiologist at UT Southwestern Medical Center, introduced Leavell to the option of a focused ultrasound treatment that was approved by the FDA in January 2026 to treat the primary motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease, including stiffness and slowness.

"High-energy ultrasound waves are focused across the skull onto discrete brain targets," Shah told Fox News Digital. "The ultrasound energy heats up these nuclei, or nerve bundles, and removes them. This stops the pathologic transmission of electrical activity causing tremors or other symptoms."

Parkinson’s patient Bud Leavell, right, shows Dr. Bhavya Shah that his hand no longer has tremors after undergoing focused ultrasound at UT Southwestern Medical Center. (UT Southwestern Medical Center)
Patients who have been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease are typically treated with medications, the doctor noted.

"Interventional options are discussed when the medications become less effective or patients develop side effects," he said. "These options include deep brain stimulation and now, focused ultrasound."
Parkinson's disease can affect patients differently, Shah pointed out.
HOW EATING HABITS COULD INFLUENCE PARKINSON’S DISEASE RISK, ACCORDING TO EXPERTS

"The beauty of focused ultrasound is that before we permanently remove the tissue, we can use low-energy ultrasound waves to see if the patient's symptoms respond to the particular target," he said. "This is very important, as the optimal target may vary in patients."
UT Southwestern also uses advanced imaging to map a patient's brain before the procedure, which gives doctors a clearer picture of the ultrasound’s intended target, according to Shah.

Parkinson’s patient Bud Leavell works on a radio at his Arlington, Texas, home. Leavell’s hand tremors have stopped since receiving focused ultrasound therapy at the UT Southwestern Medical Center. (Bud Leavell)
In Leavell's case, his tremor responded strongly even to the initial low-energy ultrasound, giving the team confidence that they had identified the right target.

"Although the cardinal symptoms of Parkinson's disease are slowness and stiffness, Bud’s most bothersome symptom was tremor, so getting rid of the shaking was our primary goal," Shah added, noting that doctors can select different brain targets based on which symptoms are most troublesome.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Leavell was eager to try the new therapy – but he did have some concerns about what the outcome would be.
"The entire team working this procedure was very professional and demonstrated considerable flexibility in making sure this was an easy process for me," he told Fox News Digital.
Immediately after receiving the ultrasound therapy on April 13, Leavell said his tremor was gone.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"I can hold my hand still with or without a tool in my hand or while working on a project," he said. "I can also get a fork or spoon with food on it into my mouth with ease. But, this may turn into another problem, as I love to eat!"
Leavell has also been able to return to his hobby of repairing antique radios.
Potential risks and tradeoffs

There are some potential risks associated with the treatment, Shah noted. Those include numbness and tingling around the mouth and fingertips, trouble walking, talking or swallowing, sometimes weakness in the upper or lower extremity, balance issues or struggles with episodic memory.
"Side effects occur approximately 20% to 30% of the time and generally improve over time," the doctor added.
Dr. Bhavya Shah monitors brain activity of Parkinson’s patient Bud Leavell as he undergoes focused ultrasound treatment at UT Southwestern Medical Center. (UT Southwestern Medical Center)

There is also one key tradeoff compared with deep brain stimulation, he noted – DBS can be adjusted if symptoms return or worsen, but with focused ultrasound, there is no device that can be reprogrammed.
That means if symptoms return after the focused ultrasound, the patient could potentially require another treatment.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Although the therapy has shown short-term effectiveness, because it is a newer technology, there is not yet long-term data available.

"For patients seeking an alternative to an implantable device, focused ultrasound represents a promising alternative," Shah said. "A patient considering these options should have a thorough discussion with their movement disorder neurologist to really understand the pros and cons of each treatment."

Parkinson’s patient Bud Leavell works on a radio at his Arlington, Texas, home. Leavell’s hand tremors have stopped since receiving focused ultrasound therapy at UT Southwestern Medical Center. (Bud Leavell)
Shah expressed optimism for the future of Parkinson’s disease therapies, with the potential for other applications of focused ultrasound.
"While this is not a panacea for Parkinson’s, it is a dramatic and life-changing procedure."
While he expressed appreciation for the procedure, Leavell emphasized that "God is in control of the circumstances in my life and will continue to be."
"However, anytime an opportunity comes along like this one, I will jump on it to see if I can experience an improvement in my circumstances."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
To anyone who may be a candidate for the focused ultrasound, Leavell recommends getting an appointment with a specialist.
"Don’t let any grass grow under your feet," he advised. "While this is not a panacea for Parkinson’s, it is a dramatic and life-changing procedure."

title: Cancer treatment delays surge across US as doctor warns system ‘needs fixing immediately’
summary: A JAMA Surgery study of over two million patients found that cancer treatment delays grew by more than 10 days across six disease types.
story: Dr. Loren Rourke, a Texas-based board-certified breast cancer surgeon, author and speaker, confirmed research has suggested that glucagon-like peptide-1 medications may be associated with a lower risk of cancer recurrence.
Wait times between a cancer diagnosis and the start of treatment grew by nearly two weeks over the past decade in the U.S., according to a recent study published in JAMA Surgery.

Researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles and Massachusetts General Hospital analyzed national data from more than two million patients diagnosed between January 2012 and December 2023.
The study tracked adults with early to locally advanced stages of six common cancers (breast, colon, lung, pancreatic, stomach and esophageal) who received surgery as part of their initial care.
WHERE YOU LIVE COULD SHAPE YOUR RISK OF CANCER MORTALITY, STUDY SUGGESTS
Researchers measured wait times from the day of the diagnosis to the first treatment, whether that was a surgery or pre-surgical therapy designed to shrink a tumor.
Across all six cancer types, median wait times grew by more than 10 days over the study period, regardless of whether surgery came first or followed other treatments.
Using National Cancer Database data from 2012 to 2023, researchers evaluated treatment delays in a cohort of over 2.7 million U.S. patients. (iStock)

The longest increases occurred in stomach cancer, where wait times rose from 35 days to 49 days, and lung cancer, which increased from 41 days to 53 days. Breast cancer wait times grew from 34 to 45 days, while colon cancer delays increased from 20 to 31 days.
CANCER WARNING SIGNS MAY APPEAR IN DNA YEARS BEFORE BLOOD TESTS DETECT TROUBLE

Pancreatic cancer waits climbed from 23 to 32 days, and esophageal cancer delays grew from 38 to 48 days. The researchers also found that a growing share of patients waited 60 days or longer to begin treatment.
"This is part of our healthcare system that needs fixing immediately," Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, told Fox News Digital.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The delays were even seen at high-volume academic medical centers, noted Siegel, who was not involved in the study.
"The waiting times for basic cancer operations in non-metastatic diseases is high and increasing since 2012," he added.
Median waiting times from diagnosis to the start of first-course therapy increased by more than 10 days across all six evaluated cancer types over the study period. (iStock)
After adjusting for factors like age and underlying health, researchers found the delays did not affect all groups in the same way.

Longer wait times were seen for Black patients, people on Medicaid, individuals in lower-income areas, patients traveling longer distances for care, and those treated at academic medical centers or high-volume hospitals.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The West experienced longer delays than other regions, and for non-breast cancers, the use of robotic surgery was linked to longer wait times.
The study authors cautioned that delays in surgical treatment have been tied to higher death rates and worse long-term survival in previous medical research.
The study authors cautioned that delays in surgical treatment have been tied to higher death rates and worse long-term survival in previous medical research. (iStock)

In supporting commentary published along with the study, Lia D. Delaney, M.D., and Sherry M. Wren, M.D., both of the Stanford School of Medicine in Palo Alto, California, emphasized that cancer care has become increasingly sophisticated over the last two decades.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
However, "as cancer care continues to regionalize, efforts to improve quality may inadvertently create barriers to timely treatment unless capacity and coordination evolve in parallel," they wrote.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The authors noted several limitations to their study. Because the analysis relied on retrospective data from the National Cancer Database, it could not determine the exact reasons behind individual treatment delays, such as scheduling issues, logistical hurdles or personal patient preferences.
The database also lacked information on when patients first developed symptoms or sought medical advice prior to diagnosis.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Brad Pitt says he can drink in ‘restrained manner’ after 7 sober years, but expert raises red flag
summary: Brad Pitt recently said he resumed drinking after seven years of sobriety, but an addiction specialist warns that "testing the waters" can be dangerous.
story: Jessica Steinman, a Los Angeles addiction specialist, generally advises against people returning to alcohol after a problematic relationship with it, warning that "testing the waters" can potentially be "dangerous."
After seven years of sobriety, Brad Pitt has revealed that he resumed drinking alcohol in moderation — an approach that has raised concerns among some addiction experts.
In an Esquire interview published on Aug. 10, the actor said, "I was sober for seven years. And then I got back off the wagon."
Pitt shared that he now drinks "in a more restrained manner," saying that he doesn’t consume "big quantities" of alcohol.
BRAD PITT ADMITS HE BEGAN DRINKING AGAIN AFTER YEARS OF SOBRIETY
"I got overconfident a couple times, went, ‘Yep, nope, not good for me,’" he acknowledged. "I have to be professional about it."
After seven years of sobriety, Brad Pitt (pictured in 2009) has revealed that he resumed drinking alcohol and now says he drinks in a "more restrained manner." (Getty Images)

Pitt once spoke about his sobriety in a 2019 New York Times interview, disclosing that he’d spent 18 months in Alcoholics Anonymous. "I had taken things as far as I could take it, so I removed my drinking privileges," he said.
BEER, WINE OR LIQUOR? MASSIVE STUDY REVEALS WHICH WAS LINKED TO LOWER DEATH RISK

Jessica Steinman, a Los Angeles addiction specialist and chief clinical officer for No Matter What Recovery, generally advises against people returning to alcohol after a problematic relationship with it, warning that "testing the waters" can potentially be "dangerous."

The National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) defines alcohol use disorder (AUD) as an impaired ability to stop or control alcohol use despite adverse social, occupational or health consequences. The condition can range from mild to severe.
Pitt shared that he now drinks "in a more restrained manner," saying that he doesn’t consume "big quantities" of alcohol. (Getty Images)

"There are people who struggle with substances and take a very large break, have a long period of sobriety and recovery, and they may choose to integrate it back into their lives," Steinman, who was not diagnosing Pitt with AUD, told Fox News Digital.
"As an addiction professional, as someone who's been in this field for a very long time, I don’t see a whole lot of success with that."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Although some people do successfully return to substances after needing to stop, Steinman considers them "anomalies and exceptions to the rule."
"People think, ‘Oh, I've gone this long. I think I'm going to be able to manage it – I have the skills now. I have tools,’" she said.
"I liken it to diabetes or heart disease – you have to manage this health issue."
Addiction can alter the brain’s reward system, she said, making it highly responsive to the dopamine release associated with drinking or substance use.

"And that doesn't go away – it lays dormant," Steinman said, comparing it to a bear in hibernation. "If you wake that bear … life can quickly become unmanageable. So they want to be very mindful of that happening."
For people with alcohol use disorder, the NIAAA says it is generally recommended to abstain from drinking for the "greatest chance of long-term success." (iStock)

The NIAAA notes that alcohol addiction involves changes across multiple brain systems related to rewards, stress, decision-making and learned responses to alcohol-related cues, and that some of those changes can continue even after drinking stops.
For those struggling with substance-use issues and mental health issues, it's a "lifelong issue" that must be managed like any other chronic illness, according to Steinman.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"I liken it to diabetes or heart disease – you have to manage this health issue," she said. "And it's the same thing for alcoholism and substance use issues."
While NIAAA acknowledges that alcohol addiction can leave some people vulnerable to relapse, the agency notes that each recovery trajectory is unique.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

For someone who has returned to drinking after a period of sobriety, Steinman said there are certain warning signs that can indicate the return of problematic patterns. Those might include escalating consumption, erratic behavior, drinking alone, secretly drinking and drinking during the day.
Moderation can also mean different things to different people, she noted.
Anyone who is noticing problematic behaviors with alcohol or drug consumption should speak with an addiction counselor. (iStock)

"Is it one drink a day? Is it a drink at dinner only? I've had people try out moderation by not having liquor at all and just sticking to beer and wine," Steinman said. "So it's all these different trials that they're doing when someone starts seeing an escalation."
Anyone who is noticing problematic behaviors with alcohol or drug consumption should speak with an addiction counselor, she advised.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
For people with alcohol use disorder, the NIAAA says it is generally recommended to abstain from drinking for the "greatest chance of long-term success."

However, the agency also notes that some people can return to occasional drinking without resuming problematic use, and says specific treatment goals should be decided between the patient and a doctor or addiction specialist.

title: Your waistline could reveal a hidden heart risk your BMI misses, major study finds
summary: Visceral fat around abdominal organs drives inflammation, insulin resistance, and artery damage in ways BMI alone cannot detect, a dietitian says.
story: Dr. Mary Claire Haver breaks down how the menopause shift rewires metabolism, raising abdominal fat and inflammation, and reveals why tracking strength and fat distribution beats relying on the number on the scale.
A person's waist size may reveal more about their heart health than the number on the scale, according to new research.
A study found that waist measurements can identify potential cardiovascular risks that may be missed when doctors rely on body mass index (BMI) alone.
Researchers from the Cross-Cohort Collaboration analyzed data from nearly 260,000 adults enrolled in 15 long-term health studies, following participants for about 20 years.
A study found that waist measurements can identify potential cardiovascular risks that may be missed when doctors rely on BMI. (iStock)
BMI IS WRONG WAY TO MEASURE OBESITY, RESEARCHERS SAY — HERE’S WHAT THEY RECOMMEND INSTEAD

The findings, published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, showed that some people considered a normal weight based on BMI still carried higher levels of fat around their midsection.

Among participants in the normal and overweight BMI ranges, those with larger waist measurements or higher waist-to-hip ratios generally faced a 15% to 50% greater risk of several heart-related problems and death during the study period, according to the study.
The results suggest that looking at how weight is distributed across the body may provide a more complete picture than BMI alone.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"BMI only tells us weight relative to height, it doesn't tell us where fat is stored, and that matters," Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based registered dietitian, certified diabetes educator and author of the book "The Sleepdemic Solution," told Fox News Digital.
Fat carried around the abdomen can pose different health concerns than fat stored elsewhere on the body, said Palinski-Wade, who was not involved in the study.

Among people with normal or overweight BMI's, larger waist sizes or higher waist-to-hip ratios were generally linked to a 15% to 50% higher risk of heart-related health problems and death during the study. (iStock)

"Where you carry fat matters more than how much you carry, because visceral fat, the fat wrapped around abdominal organs, is metabolically active tissue that drives inflammation, insulin resistance, and artery damage in a way that fat under the skin elsewhere on the body doesn't," she said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Palinski-Wade said the research highlights why BMI alone may not provide a complete picture of a person's heart health.
"BMI doesn't tell the whole story, where you carry fat may matter more than the number on the scale," she said.

Experts say the location of body fat may be more important than the overall amount. Fat stored deep in the abdomen around internal organs can promote inflammation, interfere with insulin function, and harm blood vessels. (iStock)
Researchers examined several health outcomes over the course of the study, including heart attacks, strokes, heart failure, atrial fibrillation and cardiovascular-related deaths.

In addition, the researchers noted several limitations of the study, including that they did not have information on participants' physical activity, diets or genetic risk for obesity, all of which can play a role in cardiovascular disease.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The study also measured waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio only once, limiting researchers' ability to determine how changes in abdominal fat over time may affect heart disease risk.
Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: 1 in 6 adults plagued by loneliness as researchers reveal lasting impact of COVID pandemic
summary: An Imperial College London study of over 135,000 adults found nearly one in six people reported feeling lonely often, surprising researchers. COVID made things worse, the study noted.
story: Jonathan Alpert, a New York psychotherapist, said virtual care can work very well, but that "there comes a point where a screen may not be enough."

A study of over 135,000 adults found that a surprising number of individuals feel lonely often — and that some of the loneliest people live in urban areas, shocking the researchers. Not only that — but the COVID pandemic made it worse.

Professors at Imperial College London conducted the study. They recruited a total of 135,725 volunteers aged 16 and older to complete an online survey in England throughout a five-month period in 2023.

Almost one in six adults reported feeling lonely "often or always" — and more than one in five people frequently felt a lack of companionship or had feelings of being left out or isolated, news agency SWNS reported.
WHEN IS A MENTAL HEALTH CRISIS TOO SEVERE FOR TELEHEALTH? WARNING SIGNS FAMILIES SHOULDN'T IGNORE
The findings of the study, called INTERACT, surprised those involved.
When the researchers dug deeper into the data, they found that some of the loneliest people were clustered in urban environments and cities, including London, Birmingham and Manchester.
"The key message is not simply that many people feel lonely," said the study's lead, "but that loneliness is strongly influenced by people’s surroundings, social network and environment." (iStock)

Austen El-Osta, Ph.D., public health researcher and study lead for INTERACT, said, "The key message is not simply that many people feel lonely, but that loneliness is strongly influenced by people’s surroundings, social network and their environment."

This reflected the "urban paradox" theory, the study said — where those in major cities that offer greater economic, cultural and social advantages often report lower life satisfaction, connectivity and happiness, compared to people in rural areas.
Whether people were in relationships or not didn’t seem to impact their loneliness levels, the study found.
The team also found a significant lasting effect of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Nearly 44% of respondents said the pandemic increased their feelings of loneliness — while 48.2% reported increased feelings of isolation.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Senior author of the study, Dr. Azeem Majeed of the National Health Service, said, "As an NHS GP, I see how loneliness affects both the mental and physical health of my patients. It contributes to problems such as anxiety and depression, increases the risk of long-term conditions, and often leads to more frequent GP consultations."
Nearly 44% of respondents in a new study said the COVID pandemic increased their feelings of loneliness — while 48.2% reported increased feelings of isolation. (iStock)
He said that "by strengthening community connections and social capital, we can help prevent loneliness and enable people to live healthier, happier and more connected lives."
Whether people were in relationships or not didn’t seem to impact their loneliness levels.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The research found that 45% of respondents were married or in a civil partnership — while almost 20% were single.
El-Osta said, "Loneliness is often treated as a private experience, but our findings reinforce that it is also a public health and community issue."

He added that "public health responses need to look beyond individual resilience and consider the environments, services and community assets that help people feel connected, supported and able to participate."
The research found that 45% of respondents in the study were married or in a civil partnership — while almost 20% were single. (iStock)
The team believes that this is "one of the world’s largest dedicated studies of loneliness and the largest of its kind conducted in a single country," according to Imperial College London.
The group also cautioned that while the findings offer an important snapshot, "the study cannot be used to estimate the scale of the problem at the population level."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
In addition, the researchers noted several limitations of their study, including that it overrepresented highly educated individuals and underrepresented minority ethnic groups.
They also highlighted the "inherent self-selection bias of this type of online survey, where those more interested or affected by an issue are more likely to take part."
Recently, another study found that feeling lonely may take a toll on older adults' memory — though it may not speed up cognitive decline.
Screening for loneliness should be incorporated into routine cognitive assessments as one way to support healthy aging, said researchers. (iStock)
Researchers from Colombia, Spain and Sweden analyzed data from more than 10,000 adults ages 65 to 94 across 12 European countries.
They found those who reported higher levels of loneliness did worse on memory tests at the start of the study, according to research published in the spring in the journal Aging & Mental Health.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The researchers also suggested that screening for loneliness be incorporated into routine cognitive assessments as one way to support healthy aging.
Deirdre Bardolf of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.
